title: Cera, Acolyte in Training
dek: An acolyte of Cala who helps organize a wartime burial, acknowledges the rites she does not know and completes a ceremony of temporary protection for the dead.

body:
Cera is an acolyte of Cala who accompanies a Pristinian burial party after the fighting. She is concerned with the practical work of recovering the dead and with sending them off respectfully. The scene gives her one clearly recorded task and its outcome, without supplying a whole later career.

A burial party in the mud

The adventurers meet Cera at the edge of town with four townsmen and two barrows. Rain has made the ground difficult; the men are tired and mud-covered while she waits in white and gold vestments, praying quietly. She thanks the visitors for coming.

Her first concern is how to handle the dead. Burial, burning, cairns and taking the bodies back to Phelps are all discussed. She worries that the number will overwhelm the undertaker and accepts several practical approaches so long as the dead receive dignity. She is organizing a necessary task rather than demanding one elaborate form for its own sake.

The narrator also gives a small account of her manners: her grandmother drilled politeness into her, so she does not voice her unease at Ichor’s unsettling imitation of the townsfolk’s movements.

Respect beyond the rites she knows

Cera describes Cala and Nuru as closely connected and believes that a genuine gesture in one’s name will not offend the other. She is explicit that she does not know the Rahu’s rituals. Her confidence in respectful intent is her religious judgment, not proof that she speaks for every priest or can guarantee every divine response.

The townsmen’s discussion of the earlier battle is largely rumor. Cera is going to deal with its aftermath; the scene does not make her an eyewitness to every reported act in the fighting.

The danger passes, and the dead are laid to rest

At the battlefield the party finds scavenged bodies and ghouls feeding among them. Cera shelters in the brush with the men while the adventurers deal with the threat. Once it has passed she comes forward and urges them to finish before more arrive.

The group gathers the bodies into a mass grave, covers it and marks it with a simple cairn. The narrator states that the dead are treated respectfully under her oversight. Cera prays and sprinkles holy water. In this instance, her ceremony protects those buried from becoming undead for seven days. That is a specific, temporary result, not a permanent safeguard or a universal promise about all burials.

The burial is completed. Cera’s later service, further training and whereabouts remain unestablished in the checked selection.
